titleStmt.title: Schedulability Analysis for Mixed Critical Cyber Physical Systems

analytic.title: Schedulability Analysis for Mixed Critical Cyber Physical Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Mixed criticality systems combine applications with different levels of safety within the same platform. Those applications execute under different modes, each representing an execution condition that can be required at runtime. This work proposes a mixed criticality schedulability analysis which is a modified version of the earliest deadline first scheduling paradigm. The analysis covers every possible execution condition by providing schedulability that is parametrized by the safety level. Besides, sensitivity analysis is developed for evaluating the impact of mixing criticality to schedulability and defining trade-offs between resource usage and schedulability. Test cases of real-time cyber physical systems are investigated to validate the mixed criticality analysis framework presented.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: An increasingly important trend in developing today's Cyber Physical Systems (CPS) is the integration of applications with different levels of criticality. The criticality designs the level of assurance/safety needed for a system element against failure e.g., fault, task overrun, deadline miss, [1]. In almost all standards e.g., ISO 26262, DO 178C, DO 254, IEC 61508, the definition of criticality levels is the result of failure modes and failure effects on system behavior.

The main idea with Mixed Criticality (MC) is to have safety critical applications coexisting with mission critical and non critical applications within the same system. MC tends to reconcile partitioning for safety assurance and sharing for efficient resource usage, [2].

Mixing criticality challenges both the modeling and the scheduling of real-time CPSs. Safety critical tasks have to account for the worst-case behaviors while mission critical or low critical tasks rely on less constrained/demanding models. Instead, the MC scheduling algorithms tend to guarantee timing constraints of safety critical tasks first, and then eventually accommodate less critical tasks.

The challenges to system predictability derive from the complexity of the environment that CPSs will need to operate in, coupled with emerging needs to continually increase system capabilities. The complexities of multi-and manycore [commercial-off-the-shelf] CPS implementations pose challenges in guaranteeing temporal and spacial partitioning. In particular, the difficulty stands with parameterizing such guarantees with respect to the criticality. Some of those challenges can be addressed with sensitivity and parametric analysis. They could apply to MC schedulability in order to evaluate the impact of criticality on schedulability, and define trade-offs between criticality, schedulability and resource usage.

Contribution: With this paper, we consider how resource efficient, and hence potentially commercially successful, CPS can be specified and analyzed. We develop a MC schedulability analysis from the classical earliest deadline first scheduling paradigm. It applies set of curves which bound the task behavior under different possible criticalities and it guarantee schedulability with multiple levels of assurance. The sensitivity analysis is proposed in order to evaluate the impact of MC on schedulability and trade computational resource with level of assurance. A case study of real real-time CPSs is considered to investigate the effectiveness of the MC analysis we propose. It composes of two CPSs and MC applications which are tested for the MC schedulability. The sensitivity analysis allows for an optimal computational resource usage. Organization of the Paper: In Section II we presents realtime models with bounding curves to resource requests and resource provisioning. Section III details the MC task modeling which applies bounding curves and criticality levels. Section IV illustrates both the MC scheduling and the sensitivity analysis we develop to study the effects of criticality levels on system schedulability. In Section V, the case study is applied for validating the MC framework we propose. Section VI is for concluding remarks and future work.

div.head: A. State of the Art
div.p: Safety critical tasks have to account for the worst-case behaviors that can possibly happen. The models for safety critical tasks have to assure the coverage of any of the execution conditions, worst-cases with fault effects included. Mission critical or low critical applications rely on less constrained models for which the guarantees are not as strict as those for safety critical applications, [3], [4].

To model MC tasks it is possible to apply the real-time calculus and time interval representations [5], [6] that consider curves to bound task and resource behavior under different execution conditions, [7], [8].

MC systems are defined to execute in a number of criticality modes and todays existing MC scheduler relies on mode changes, [9], [10], [11], [12]. Once the system is in high criticality mode, only high criticality tasks are scheduled and all the other tasks are dropped. The MC schedulability test we propose makes use of classical scheduler such as Earliest Deadline First (EDF) [6]. It applies MC task models and resource partitions for schedulability conditions that depend on the desired level of assurance. The resource usage is optimized by scheduling the maximum possible number of tasks together.

The industry perspective to the MC problem focuses more on partitioning and separating applications by their criticality level. Safety critical applications would be timely and/or spacey separated from mission critical applications, [13], [14]; both models and schedulability are guaranteed within the partition.

Finally, the sensitivity analysis applies to task models in order to study the impact that task parameters have on schedulability, [15], [16]. The sensitivity analysis is applicable to MC problems for CPSs in order to evaluate the impact of criticality levels on schedulability and then to optimize the resource usage. Effective sensitivity analysis has yet to be built for the MC scheduling problem.

div.head: II. COMPUTATIONAL MODELS
div.p: A real-time task τ i consists of a sequence of recurring jobs, each to be executed before a given deadline. The task model can be represented with the tuple (T i , D i , C i ), τ i = (T i , D i , C i ), with T i the task period or minimum interarrival time, D i the task deadline and C i the task Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET). Tasks are grouped into task sets Γ, or real-time applications, Γ = {τ 1 , . . . , τ n }.

For a task τ i activated at time t = 0, the resource bound function rbf i (t) in any interval [0, t], rbf i (t) = max 0, t Ti • C i , defines an upper bound to any cumulative resource request that τ i might request for executing, [5].

The computational resource used to execute tasks is provided by reservation mechanisms, also known as servers. The resource provisioning of a server can be lower bounded in [0, t] with the supply bound function (sbf) sbf. sbf S (t) is the minimum amount of time provided by server S in any interval of length t ≥ 0, [17], [18].

div.head: A. Real-Time Scheduling
div.p: A common preemptive scheduling policy is EDF [6], where each job has a fixed priority assigned according to its deadline. The EDF schedulability is guaranteed if the computational resource that a task set requires to execute by the deadlines is less than or equal to the available computational resource.

The set of time instances where to check EDF schedulability can be reduced to the set D of deadlines within the task set hyperperiod, [6]. The demand bound function (dbf) of τ i , dbf i , is the resource requested by τ i to fully execute by its deadline, dbf i (t) = rbf i (t -D i ). dbf Γ is the resource demand of the whole task set Γ: dbf Γ = Γ dbf i , as the cumulative resource demand. This work applies mostly to single-core processors. With resource partitioning, like virtualization platforms/hypervisors, and minor modifications to take into account the delay effects from resource competition, this work can fit multi-core platforms also. Moreover, this work focuses on EDF scheduling but similar reasoning can be applied to fixed priority scheduling.

div.head: III. MIXED CRITICALITY MODELING
div.p: In MC real-time systems, parameters such as the WCET depend on the criticality level that has to be assured for each task, [3].

Safety critical applications have to be assured against any possible execution condition, faults included. A piece of code could have a higher WCET if it is defined to be safety critical with higher level of assurance required. Instead, if the task is just considered to be mission critical or non-critical, its WCET requirement would be smaller, as the task demands less in terms of resource request and guarantees, [3], [21], [4]. In this work, we restrict our modeling and analysis to two criticality levels, the high criticality HI and the low criticality LO, although the reasoning can generalize to any criticality level.

• C i (HI) models the HI-criticality behavior of the system, thus the worst possible conditions τ i can suffer; C i (HI) would be derived from the most safe timing analysis in order to guarantee the worst model and the most assurance to the execution behavior, [21]; C i (HI) has to be the task model with maximum confidence of being the worst-case, [3] • C i (LO) models the LO-criticality conditions for τ i ;

C i (LO) is for mission critical or less-critical conditions; it does not assure against faults, at least it does not against all of them; C i (LO) could come from less safe timing analysis and encode a certain confidence to be the worstcase model under specific execution conditions [3]; it can also be associated with a threshold probability [21].

By MC constraints, it has to be C i (HI) ≥ C i (LO), [3]. In a MC paradigm, it is possible to distinguish between HI- criticality tasks from LO-criticality tasks such that: HI-criticality tasks can have two execution modes, HIcriticality mode and LO-criticality mode, represented by
div.formula: [C i (HI), C i (LO)]. The MC HI-criticality task model is: τ i = ([C i (HI), C i (LO)], T i , D i ),
div.p: where HI and LO WCETs represent respectively the HI-criticality mode bounded by C i (HI) and the LO-criticality mode bounded by C i (LO). In the industrial MC task model, it could be τ i = (C i (HI), T i , D i ) with only the HI-criticality mode bounded. LO-criticality tasks can only executes under LO-criticality mode; for them, only C i (LO) is necessary to bound their behavior. The MC LO-criticality task model is:
div.formula: τ i = (C i (LO), T i , D i ).
div.p: In our MC computational model, we assume that all HI- criticality tasks move to HI-criticality mode at the same time, [22], [12]. This is a common assumption in MC scheduling which allows for easier schedulability tests. On the other hand, it overestimate the resource provisioning with too pessimistic results with respect to the real behavior where fewer HI-criticality tasks can change mode. Task Set Partitioning. The task set Γ can be partitioned into Γ HI and Γ LO , Γ = Γ HI ∪ Γ LO , where Γ HI contains all the HIcriticality tasks, and Γ LO contains the LO-criticality tasks. The criticality level cl describes the assurance level required for both Γ HI and Γ LO at runtime; it reflects the criticality mode as well as the safety/criticality required at runtime. A HI- criticality task τ i can have two criticality modes HI-criticality and LO-criticality, and its runtime criticality level cl HI,i can assume one of them, cl HI,i ∈ {HI, LO}. Since it is assumed that all tasks within Γ HI move to HI-criticality mode at the same time, then Γ HI criticality level cl HI can be HI-criticality or LO-criticality, cl HI ∈ {HI, LO}. With Γ LO , only the LOcriticality level is possible which means that for those tasks, only LO-criticality assurances can be provided, cl HI it is associated the LO criticality level. We consider also the dbf resulting from combinations of HI-criticality and LOcriticality tasks, which is our way of considering both HI and LO-criticality tasks for schedulability.

div.head: IV. SCHEDULING WITH MIXED CRITICALITY
div.p: The MC scheduling policy we propose applies EDF to mixed criticality models. The EDF-based MC scheduling algorithm, MC-EDF, is a minor contribution to MC scheduling but it allows defining a flexible schedulability condition which is parametrized with criticality levels; it makes use of dbf and sbf.

The first objective of MC-EDF is to find which are the criticality levels that can be assured schedulable with Γ HI , Γ LO and combinations among them. The second objective is to evaluate the resource applied to execute Γ HI , and thus the resource left to execute Γ LO tasks without harming HIcriticality tasks.

By its nature, MC-EDF tends to close the gap between the research perspective and the industrial perspective to the MC scheduling problem, since it avoids LO-criticality task dropping and maximizes resource utilization.

div.head: B. Sensitivity Analysis for MC
div.p: The sensitivity analysis, applied to task parameters and realtime scheduling, tries to respond to questions like: i) what is the total resource request that can be accommodated with the given resource provisioning? ii) How much the resource provisioning can be changed in order to make the application schedulable? [15], [23] With the MC schedulability condition of Theorem 1 together with the (α, Δ)-space representation, the sensitivity analysis can be applied in order to evaluate the impact that criticality levels have on task schedulability. The sensitivity analysis can be used to identify the most schedulable criticality levels, to quantify the cost (in terms of resource usage) of making a specific criticality level schedulable and to quantify the amount of resource left in order to safely schedule extra tasks e.g., LO- criticality tasks.

-MC scheduling: From the schedulability level and bounds, it is possible to quantify how many and which LO-criticality tasks can be executed concurrently with HI-criticality tasks without jeopardizing them all. Given a sbf, the criticality levels that can be guaranteed come from Theorem 1 and the schedulability regions of the (α, Δ)-space.

-Resource evaluation: It is possible defining changes in the resource provisioning in order to include other levels into system schedulability. With the Euclidean distance for the (α, Δ)-space, it is possible evaluating beforehand the amount of change necessary to the desired criticality level schedulability. Being (α 1 , Δ 1 ) the initial resource and (α 2 , Δ 2 ) the final resource, the distance can be defined such that (δα = α 2α 1 , δΔ = Δ 2 -Δ 1 ). Some changes could aim at minimizing the α variation (δα = α 2α 1 , δΔ = 0) or minimizing the Δ variation (δα = α 2α 1 , δΔ = 0).
Those are ways we enforce for investigating the criticality and schedulability trade-off as well as the resource usage and schedulability trade-off.

The sensitivity analysis, applied to study the MC schedulability, provides useful feedback to conceive and develop embedded systems. This is particularly important with CPSs and todays implementation platforms where resource efficiency is critical. Fig. 3. Example of sensitivity analysis; α is on the x axis, Δ is on the y axis. div.head: V. CASE STUDY
div.p: The MC schedulability and sensitivity analysis are applied into two CPSs. They allow to clarify the MC analysis framework proposed and verify its applicability to real applications.

div.head: A. Test Case 1 -Control Application ROSACE
div.p: The test case hereby analyzed is the CPS application ROSACE, http://sites.onera.fr/schedmcore/ROSACE and https://svn.onera.fr/schedmcore/branches/ schedmcore-RTAS2014/Case Study RTAS/, which is a multi-periodic controller executing on a multi/many-core target. It composes of 11 tasks τ 1 . . . τ 11 , all HI-criticality tasks, with precedence constraints which have been removed here with the use of backlogs to guarantee data integrity. Those tasks exploits processing, sensing and actuation elements of the CPS; they are relatively light tasks, expect τ 7 , with small utilization. The task utilization is the ratio between task WCET and task period, U i = C i /T i .. The HI-criticality tasks have two modes, HI-and LO-criticality modes.

To the original ROSACE task set, we added 3 LO-criticality tasks (τ 12 , τ 13 , τ 14 ). They represent less critical jobs such as image processing or others, that we want to integrate in the same platform; they have only one mode i.e. LO- criticality mode. All three tasks are heavy in order to represent expensive but non-functional operations. We call the resulting CPS ROSACE++. Table I resumes the whole application and the task parameters.

At first we try analyzing the whole application as a single partition with an initial resource of sbf 1 = (0.7, 20), see Table I. sbf 1 is able to guarantee schedulability of all HIcriticality tasks in LO-criticality mode plus any combination of the LO-criticality tasks, even all the tasks together. Only a resource of sbf 2 = (0.95, 5), see Table I, is able to guarantee the schedulability of HI-criticality tasks in HIcriticality mode. This comes with a cost of resource change of δα = 0.95-0.7 = 0.2 and δΔ = 5-20 = -15. A negative δΔ means a reduction of idle time, thus more resource to be provided. Figure 4 illustrates the case.

Whenever in HI-criticality mode, only τ 12 can be guaranteed executing with the HI-criticality tasks, case HI-1 in Figure 4. For that happening, a resource of sbf 3 = (1, 0) would be necessary, being the utilization of such combination 198/200.

The second CPS design we can consider consists of partitioning the application. A first partition is P 1 = {τ 1 , τ 4 , τ 5 , τ 6 , τ 7 , τ 9 , τ 12 } and a second partition is P 2 = {τ 2 , τ 3 , τ 8 , τ 10 , τ 11 , τ 13 , τ 14 }. In terms of utilization, P 1 is such that U 1,HI-1 HI = 188/200, when the HI-criticality tasks are in HI-criticality mode; P 2 is such that U 2,HI-2 HI = 135/200 when HI-criticality tasks are in HI-criticality mode. In terms of resource, per partition there are two possible resource availability: sbf 1 1 = (0.4, 20) and sbf 1 2 = (0.8, 5) for P1, sbf 2 1 = (0.8, 38), sbf 2 2 = (0.8, 11) for P2, see Table I. Figure 5 illustrates the partitions, each with the available resources. , it is possible to guarantee all the tasks in P1, see Figure 5(a) where only some of the bounds are represented. In it, HI stands for all the HI-criticality tasks in HI-criticality mode plus τ 12 , while LO stands for the all the HI-criticality tasks in LO-criticality mode plus τ 12 . The cost for the full schedulability within P1, guaranteed by sbf 1 2 , is δα = 0.4 and δΔ = -15, see Figure 5(a). We remind that full schedulability means that LO-criticality tasks can execute concurrently with HI-criticality tasks without jeopardizing any timing constraint.

With P2, sbf 2 1 guarantees all the tasks, but with the HIcriticality in LO-criticality mode (LO-6 case in Figure 5(b)). Instead, with sbf 2 1 , it is also possible to schedule all the HIcriticality tasks in P2 in HI-criticality modes; in that case, τ 13 and τ 14 have to be dropped. By increasing the resource to sbf 1 2 , it is possible to guarantee all the tasks in P2 in HIcriticality mode (HI-6), see Figure 5(b). The cost for the full schedulability within P2 is δα = 0 and δΔ = -27. The partitioned solution can be implemented with a dual core platform.

Another partitioning solution could be such that all HI- criticality tasks are together but separated from all the LO- criticality tasks. This is more the industry approach to the MC problem, which would end up into less efficient resource utilization.

div.head: B. Test Case 2: Robotic Application
div.p: The CPS we consider now is a robotic application from the MAUVE project https://forge.onera.fr/projects/mauve. It composes of 8 tasks τ 1 , . . . τ 8 which describe all the main functionality of a robot e.g., SLAM, navigation, control, tracking. All those tasks represent two different criticality levels, since they are different in terms of assurance and importance for the robot functionality. We name HI-criticality tasks and MI-criticality tasks to distinguish between safety critical tasks (HI-criticality such as "control" and "guidance" tasks) and mission critical tasks (MI-criticality such as "camera" and "navigation" tasks).

To those, we added 7 LO-criticality tasks τ 9 , . . . τ 15 which are non-critical at all, but they are applied to increase the load of the platform with other non-functional elements. Table II resumes all the task parameters. To note that for this case, we have assumed just one mode per criticality level. This is a more industrial perspective to the MC problem where HI- criticality tasks are represented with a single WCET, although large. The criticality levels here come from the combinations between HI/MI and LO-criticality tasks.

div.p: We propose the MC scheduling which applies to the EDF scheduling paradigm. The MC schedulability test makes use of multiple bounding curves and the schedulability is guaranteed depending on the available resource and the desired criticality level. The MC sensitivity analysis is developed to study the impact of criticality on schedulability and exploring trade-offs.

The evaluation section studies real MC CPSs. It shows how MC scheduling and MC sensitivity analysis allow for resource optimization and schedulability conditions that guarantee both HI-criticality tasks and LO-criticality tasks.

Future work will explore policies to optimize resource changes and to guarantee criticality levels. Furthermore, other parameters than WCETs will be applied into sensitivity analysis in order to leverage trade-offs for the design of CPSs.
